citation: Furthermore, gap years provide opportunities for practical skill development.  A student might undertake a coding bootcamp, a wilderness first responder course, or a marketing internship – experiences that directly translate into marketable skills. This ‘stackable credentialing’ – accumulating skills and certifications outside of traditional academic pathways – is becoming increasingly recognized by employers (Autor, 2022).  A gap year, therefore, can be viewed as a form of experiential learning, bridging the gap between academic theory and real-world application. This is especially relevant given the increasing popularity of alternative credentialing programs and micro-credentials.

best_near.title: The number of online courses, programs, and schools are growing exponentially in K-12 education.  Given the unique nature of online courses and the distinct skills necessary to create a quality online course, it is essential that effective professional development be provided for teachers designing online courses.  Given the need for these courses to be of the same quality as their face-to-face counter parts, K-12 teachers must learn how to design an online course to meet recognized standards of quality.  The present study explored the effects of a professional development model designed to provide an authentic, project and standards-based experience to K-12 educators.  The extent to which teachers designed an online module to meet Quality Matters standards was assessed.  Overall, the majority of participants (n=97) were able to successfully transfer learning to design and develop an online course to meet standards.  Areas of concern regarding specific standards are discussed.  Recommendations for more rigorous research are suggested to determine the degree to which outcomes are specifically related to the course experience as opposed to outside variables such as learner and instructor characteristics.  Results of this study can be used to inform design of effective professional development for online course design.

citation: Community-led adaptation is equally critical. Top-down, externally driven adaptation projects are often less effective than those designed and implemented in collaboration with local communities who possess invaluable traditional knowledge and a deep understanding of their environment. In many Pacific Islands, traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) guides sustainable resource management and disaster preparedness. For example, traditional building techniques employ materials and designs that are naturally resilient to storms and floods. Integrating TEK with modern scientific knowledge creates more effective and culturally appropriate adaptation strategies (Berkes, 2012).  Participatory vulnerability assessments, where communities actively identify their risks and priorities, are a core component of this approach.
